Constitutional Balance of Power.dimension_summary: Constitutional Balance of Power remained in mild concern, with executive precedent holding at a steady concern level, from the President's claim he could issue $5,000 “dividend” checks without Congress to a second contested pocket rescission of $810 million. The dimension improved substantially from August, driven by judicial review: the Supreme Court intervened three times to block Missouri's redrawn congressional map and blocked the administration's mail-ballot restrictions. Legislative processes also gained, as Congress affirmed that the dividend payments would require its approval, saw impeachment articles filed against Defense Secretary Hegseth, held Leon Black in contempt, and passed a Russia sanctions bill, though the Senate fell one vote short of ending the Iran war.

weekly_explainers.text: This factor tracks whether subnational governments retain and exercise meaningful authority against federal control. States and localities pushed back against the federal government on several fronts this week. New York Governor Kathy Hochul pardoned Keisy Guerrero Mariano, a noncitizen with a criminal conviction whose case was pending before the U.S. Supreme Court; the pardon ended the case — which asked whether the federal government may detain immigrants with serious convictions for months without a bond hearing — and the Court dismissed it on September 11, a month before oral argument. In Colorado, Jefferson County became one of a few school districts to sue the Trump administration over its demand that districts revoke transgender protections or lose federal funding. The city of Denver, joined by Latino civil rights groups, sued the Department of Homeland Security to bar Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers from polling places during the midterms, invoking a Civil War–era “troops at the polls” law after Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said earlier this month that ICE was authorized to be present. And New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill defended the state’s sanctuary limits on local-federal immigration cooperation. California enacted more than a dozen laws restricting addictive social-media features and AI chatbots, and a Texas court ruled that TikTok had misled parents about its safety tools, while the federal government deliberately held to a light-touch posture rather than issuing rules of its own. In each case, subnational actors asserted their own authority rather than deferring to Washington.

Sub-national autonomy holds up when states and localities actively assert their own authority rather than deferring reflexively to Washington. California Governor Newsom signed a package of bills explicitly meant to prevent federal interference in the state’s midterm elections and barred other states’ National Guard units from operating in California without his consent. Multiple states and cities separately sued the administration over its new rule stating that use of public assistance can render one ineligible for a green card.

States Push Back as Washington Presses
A federal system works when states and cities can set their own policy and challenge Washington without punishment. California and New York sued over the administration’s push to halt wind energy projects, and Gov. Kathy Hochul rejected a Justice Department demand to lift New York’s handgun-sale ban for 18-to-20-year-olds. Pressure ran the other way too: DOJ sued Minnesota over its gun-purchase waiting period, a federal voting arrest became a flashpoint in Gov. Mikie Sherrill’s fights with the administration, and the New York City Council dropped a benefits auto-enrollment plan over immigrant privacy fears.

weekly_explainers.text: This factor measures how well the system insulates itself from hostile foreign intervention. Reporting this week described adversaries turning American-built artificial-intelligence tools against US interests — used to develop weapons and electronic-warfare tools targeting Taiwan, to attempt targeting of US Navy ships, and to develop guidance and control software for rockets and ballistic and hypersonic missiles. Separately, Chinese intelligence-sharing was linked to an Iranian missile strike that killed three US service members.

A democracy’s decisions need to reflect its own citizens’ will rather than the interests of foreign governments working to shape outcomes covertly, which is why foreign assassination plots, financial entanglements, and disinformation efforts targeting the US are treated as direct threats to self-governance. The most consequential story here involved the Justice Department charging five men in Russia-backed plots to assassinate Ukrainian allies on U.S. soil, with the FBI saying it had disrupted at least one planned killing in Washington, D.C. NHL star Alex Ovechkin also drew attention, including from a Republican congressman, after appearing in a campaign ad supporting Putin. Reports also emerged suggesting that Russia intends to interfere in US elections, sparking a Congressional inquiry. Questions also emerged across the media when it was revealed this week that a Russian businessman had funded Trump Jr.’s wedding festivities, particularly as Trump’s son-in-law Kushner has been actively involved in peace negotiations between Russia and Ukraine, among other conflicts.

External influence considers whether foreign governments can shape American politics through gifts, espionage, or other forms of interference. Sen. John Curtis urged a Senate committee to investigate Donald Trump Jr. after reports emerged suggesting that a Putin-linked oligarch helped pay for his wedding, and prosecutors said a Russian-owned company deceived the Secret Service to win contracts. The Pentagon is actively addressing the issue of fighter jets being diverted to Hong Kong and seized by Chinese authorities, while Trump reportedly softened his stance toward China after earlier accusing it of election meddling. Sen. Dave McCormick said China and Russia are fueling the domestic data-center backlash, in an effort to win the global race on AI development and expansion.

weekly_explainers.text: This factor tracks the stability of relations across governments and international bodies. The president’s break with longstanding US neutrality on Irish unification provoked strong reactions with allies across the political spectrum. The deepening tariff dispute with Canada further strained the relationship between the two countries. The war in Iran continued, with increasingly high stakes for the global economy (see also National Economic Security). However, the potential for increased cooperation may open up through proposed trilateral US–Russia–Ukraine talks.

Alliance Strain with Canada, Strength Elsewhere
Relations with Canada and the EU deteriorated sharply this week: as Canada’s leadership pursued a “unique alliance” with the EU amid the ongoing trade war with the US. The White House called the idea “laughable” while threatening tariffs and warned Europe the move could be treated as a hostile act. Elsewhere, US alliances held: NATO jets shot down a Russian drone that violated Lithuanian airspace, while Israel and Morocco moved to open embassies in a reaffirmation of the Abraham Accords and a US envoy secured the release of 25 more prisoners in Belarus.

President Trump signed a security deal with Denmark and Greenland that lets the US build two military bases in the Arctic while reaffirming Danish sovereignty. US and Chinese officials opened communications on AI risks ahead of Xi Jinping’s state visit, extending the trade negotiations. US envoys held three hours of talks with Iran outside of UN General Assembly meetings, Ukraine’s president said Trump agreed to let his country produce Patriot missiles, and Trump met with new British Prime Minister Andy Burnham. Strains remained, including Trump’s rejection of Iran’s Hormuz proposal and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s disclosure that he prepared for the remote chance of US military action.

Sovereign Relations.dimension_summary: Sovereign Relations remained in mild concern, driven by a sharp rise in foreign-interference concerns, including adversaries using American AI tools for weapons development, Russia-backed assassination plots on U.S. soil, and reports that a Putin-linked oligarch helped pay for Donald Trump Jr.'s wedding. The dimension still improved from August as states asserted their authority, with Governor Hochul's pardon ending a pending Supreme Court immigration case, California enacting protections against federal interference in its midterms, and states suing over the green card rule and the halt to wind projects. Intergovernmental cooperation also recovered late in the month with a Greenland security deal with Denmark and renewed talks with China and Iran, after strain with Canada and the EU earlier.
